questionText: How do IEnumerable<T>, IEnumerator<T>, and yield return work together?
shortAnswer: IEnumerable<T> provides GetEnumerator(); the enumerator's MoveNext/Current walks items; yield return makes the compiler generate that state machine for you, producing lazy, one-at-a-time sequences.
detailedAnswer: foreach needs only GetEnumerator() + MoveNext() + Current — duck-typed in the pattern, interface-backed for abstraction. Hand-writing an enumerator means a class tracking position and version (fail-fast). yield return automates it: the compiler emits a state-machine class capturing locals, resuming after each yield and running finally blocks on disposal (early loop exit disposes → finally runs — resource cleanup works). Laziness consequences: no work happens until enumerated (a yielded DB query runs at foreach, not at call); exceptions throw at enumeration, not at method call (validate eagerly, yield lazily: public wrapper validates then calls a private iterator); re-enumeration re-executes everything (double SQL queries — materialize with ToList when reused); infinite sequences are expressible (while(true) yield) but must be Take-bounded. yield break ends early. No yield in try/catch with return... precisely: yield is forbidden inside try-catch (allowed in try-finally). Async twin: IAsyncEnumerable<T> + await foreach + CancellationToken ([EnumeratorCancellation]). Prefer iterators for pipelines/parsers; materialize at trust/API boundaries.
internalWorking: The compiler generates a <EvenNumbers>d__ class implementing IEnumerable+IEnumerator with a state int; MoveNext is a switch jumping to resume points; locals become fields. finally blocks compile into the Dispose path — breaking mid-foreach still cleans up. No allocation beyond the one state-machine object per GetEnumerator call.
realWorldUsage: Line readers, CSV row streams, paginated API walkers, tree traversals, test-data builders, and chunked ETL without loading everything.
commonMistake: Validation inside the iterator (throws late — split eager/deferred), enumerating twice (double cost — ToList once), mutating the source mid-iteration (version exception), and yield inside try-catch (compile error — restructure).
technicalConversation: Ask where the exception surfaces if the file is missing — at the call or the foreach? The answer (foreach) motivates the eager-validation wrapper pattern.
interviewFollowUp: How do finally blocks behave when a consumer breaks out of foreach early?
keyTakeaway: yield = compiler-written lazy state machine. Validate eagerly, enumerate thoughtfully, materialize at boundaries.

questionText: When should you inherit from Collection<T> instead of exposing List<T>?
shortAnswer: Inherit Collection<T> when you need virtual hooks (InsertItem/SetItem/RemoveItem/ClearItems) for validation or notifications; otherwise expose List<T> privately and publish IReadOnlyList<T>. Never inherit List<T> — its members aren't virtual, so overrides silently don't run.
detailedAnswer: List<T> methods are non-virtual: class Validated : List<T> with a 'checked Add' compiles but Add calls bind to List.Add (hiding, not overriding) — callers through List<T> references bypass validation entirely. Collection<T> exists for this: protected virtual InsertItem/SetItem/RemoveItem/ClearItems funnel every mutation, so ObservableCollection<T> (which extends Collection<T>) raises change events reliably. Pattern: class RangeChecked : Collection<int> { protected override void InsertItem(int i, int v) { Validate(v); base.InsertItem(i, v); } } — works through IList<T> references too. For most code, composition beats both: private List<T> field + IReadOnlyList<T> property (or AsReadOnly live view). Expose Collection<T> from APIs when callers should mutate with your rules; expose IReadOnly* when they shouldn't. Immutable alternative: ImmutableList<T> (structural sharing, every mutation returns a new instance — thread-safe by design, O(log n) ops). Rule: inherit for behavior hooks, compose for storage, immutable for sharing.
internalWorking: Collection<T> stores items in an IList<T> (List<T> by default) and routes Add/Insert/Remove/Clear/setter through the virtual hooks — one indirection per mutation, negligible. List<T> calls bind statically (callvirt on non-virtual = direct), hence the bypass.
realWorldUsage: Validated domain collections (non-empty tags, ranged scores), observable UI collections, and EF navigation backing fields (which need hook-free plain collections — use List/HashSet there, not custom).
commonMistake: Inheriting List<T> for validation (silently bypassed), overriding without calling base (items vanish), and exposing Collection<T> setters publicly (callers replace the whole collection — expose getter-only).
technicalConversation: Ask them to predict the alias.Add(-5) outcome before running — the surprise teaches virtual-dispatch requirements permanently.
interviewFollowUp: How does ObservableCollection<T> use these hooks, and what breaks if you bypass them?
keyTakeaway: List<T> is not designed for inheritance. Collection<T> gives virtual mutation hooks; composition covers the rest.

questionText: What is the difference between AsReadOnly, ToList, and ToArray when exposing collections?
shortAnswer: AsReadOnly wraps the live list (no copy — later mutations show through); ToList/ToArray snapshot (copy now — immune to later changes). Return snapshots across trust/async boundaries; live views only for tightly-coupled same-owner scenarios.
detailedAnswer: ReadOnlyCollection<T> (list.AsReadOnly()) is a wrapper: O(1), no allocation of elements, but reflects subsequent adds/removes — callers see your internals move (fine for UI bound to an ObservableCollection you own; dangerous across threads or awaits). ToList()/ToArray() copy: O(n) once, then fully independent — safe to cache, return from async methods, or hand to untrusted code. Arrays from ToArray are exactly sized (no spare capacity, unlike List's buffer). Array.Empty<T>() for the empty case (singleton, no allocation). IReadOnlyList<T> as the declared type hides mutability either way — but document live-vs-snapshot semantics in XML docs, because the same interface behaves differently (a consumer caching a 'read-only' live view gets stale-data bugs). Builder pattern: accept List internally, expose IReadOnlyList via AsReadOnly at the end when ownership is clear. Records/DTOs: ToList snapshots in constructors (freeze at the boundary). Cost awareness: snapshotting a million-item list per request is a real allocation — for hot paths, expose the live read-only view or paginate.
internalWorking: ReadOnlyCollection<T> holds the IList<T> reference and forwards indexers/Count; the JIT devirtualizes the wrapper for sealed paths. ToList allocates via ICollection<T>.Count fast-path (exact size, single copy); ToArray identical. AsReadOnly on arrays returns the same wrapper type (arrays are already fixed-size).
realWorldUsage: Repository returns (snapshots), ViewModel-bound live collections, cached reference data (snapshot once), and DTO construction at API boundaries.
commonMistake: Returning the live wrapper from async/cached code (races + drift), snapshotting huge lists per request (GC churn — expose views or pages), and null collections (return empty, never null).
technicalConversation: Ask whether their cached reference data is a snapshot or a live view — if they can't answer, the semantics were never decided, and that is the bug class.
interviewFollowUp: When is a live read-only view preferable to a snapshot, despite the aliasing?
keyTakeaway: AsReadOnly = live window, ToList/ToArray = frozen photo. Snapshot across boundaries; document which you chose.

questionText: What are ImmutableArray<T>, ImmutableList<T>, and ImmutableDictionary<K,V>, and when do they pay off?
shortAnswer: Persistent collections where every 'mutation' returns a new instance sharing most structure (O(log n) via trees/tries). They pay off for shared snapshots across threads, undo/history, and lock-free reads — at the cost of slower writes and API ceremony versus List/Dictionary.
detailedAnswer: System.Collections.Immutable provides: ImmutableArray<T> (struct wrapper over array — the fastest immutable: O(1) index, copy-on-write via SetItem; default (uninitialized) instances throw — always initialize with .Empty), ImmutableList<T> (balanced tree, O(log n) add/remove/index), ImmutableDictionary/HashSet (HAMT tries, O(log n) with tiny constants), ImmutableQueue/Stack (O(1) amortized, ideal for persistent BFS/DFS), and builders (ImmutableList.CreateBuilder() — mutate locally, ToImmutable() once — List-like speed during construction). Sharing: two versions share all but the changed path, so snapshots are O(1)-ish memory. Threading: lock-free reads/writes by construction (publish via Interlocked.Exchange of the reference). Costs: per-op constants 2–5x mutable equivalents; ToImmutable() on hot paths allocates the tree. Use when: snapshots cross threads (config, routing tables published atomically), undo stacks, event-sourced state rebuilds, or APIs promising no-mutation. Avoid for: tight mutation loops (use List + ToImmutable at the end), large primitive grids (arrays/spans win), and EF entities (change tracking needs mutability).
internalWorking: ImmutableList is an AVL tree (branching 32 in practice via node arrays); ImmutableDictionary a hash-array-mapped-trie (32-way). Path copying clones O(log n) nodes per write; the rest is shared (GC-friendly — shared nodes survive together). ImmutableArray is just T[] + structural wrapper (no tree — fastest, least flexible).
realWorldUsage: Roslyn syntax trees (the canonical use), snapshotted configuration, undo buffers, multi-version caches, and concurrent snapshot publishing.
commonMistake: default(ImmutableArray<T>) use (throws — always .Empty), per-item Add in loops without builders (log-factor churn), and expecting mutation (v1.Add doesn't change v1 — reassign!).
technicalConversation: Ask how they would publish a routing table to 64 reader threads with zero locks — Interlocked.Exchange of an ImmutableDictionary reference is the one-line answer.
interviewFollowUp: Why is ImmutableArray a struct, and what failure mode does that create?
keyTakeaway: Mutations return new shared-structure versions. Builders for construction, trees for sharing, arrays for speed.

questionText: What are FrozenDictionary and FrozenSet (.NET 8), and when should you freeze a collection?
shortAnswer: FrozenDictionary<K,V>/FrozenSet<T> (.NET 8, System.Collections.Frozen) are built once via ToFrozenDictionary() and optimized for ultra-fast reads (perfect hashing, no mutation API). Freeze static/reference data read millions of times: routes, MIME maps, keyword tables, config lookups.
detailedAnswer: Construction analyzes the data and picks the layout: tiny sets → linear scan (beating hashing below ~10 items), small → hash table, large string keys → length-segmented perfect-ish hashing with vectorized compares. Reads are 20–50% faster than Dictionary with zero mutation surface (no Add/Remove — construction only). Patterns: static readonly FrozenSet<string> Keywords = new[]{...}.ToFrozenSet(StringComparer.Ordinal); routes and MIME maps as FrozenDictionary; tests use the same builders. Comparers flow through (ToFrozenDictionary(k => k, v => v, StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)). Costs: slower construction (analysis + layout — one-time) and no mutation (rebuild to change — fine for static data, wrong for caches; use ConcurrentDictionary/MemoryCache there). Lookup with fallback: frozen.TryGetValue else compute. AOT/trimming friendly (no reflection). Benchmarks: freeze anything on a hot read path with a fixed key set — the win is consistent across key types, largest for short strings.
internalWorking: At freeze time the builder measures key distribution: chooses ValuesFrozenSet (linear), HashFrozenSet, or LengthBucketsFrozenSet (groups by string length, then hashes within buckets — kills most collisions). Reads are branch-light with SIMD key compares where applicable. No version field, no mutation paths — smaller objects, hotter cache.
realWorldUsage: MIME maps, route tables, keyword/operator sets in parsers, country/currency tables, feature-flag name sets, and DI service-name lookups.
commonMistake: Freezing per-request data (construction cost dwarfs the win — freeze once statically), expecting mutation (rebuild instead), and freezing tiny maps where a switch expression would be faster and clearer.
technicalConversation: Ask what in their request path is a fixed lookup rebuilt every time — static data constructed per request is the freeze candidate hiding in most codebases.
interviewFollowUp: Why does freezing pick different layouts by size, and where is the crossover roughly?
keyTakeaway: Build once, read millions of times. Freeze static lookup data; never freeze caches or per-request maps.

questionText: How do SortedDictionary, SortedList, and SortedSet differ, and when is ordering worth the cost?
shortAnswer: All keep keys sorted: SortedDictionary (red-black tree, O(log n), fast inserts), SortedList (two arrays, O(n) inserts but O(1)/binary-search reads + index access), SortedSet (ordered unique set + range views). Pay O(log n) only when you need ordered traversal, ranges, or neighbors.
detailedAnswer: SortedDictionary<K,V>: red-black tree — O(log n) add/remove/lookup, no index access, enumerates sorted; best for mixed workloads needing order. SortedList<K,V>: parallel key/value arrays kept sorted — O(n) insert/remove (memmove) but binary-search lookup, O(1) index access (ElementAt without walking), lowest memory — best for build-once, read-many ordered maps (config tables loaded at startup). SortedSet<T>: ordered unique values with Min/Max, GetViewBetween(min, max) live range views, Reverse(), and set ops (UnionWith etc. preserving order) — leaderboards, schedules, interval management. All take IComparer<T> (StringComparer, custom). Neighbors: SortedSet predecessor/successor via views; dictionaries lack them (use SortedList index ± 1). Costs vs HashSet/Dictionary: O(log n) vs O(1), plus comparer calls per step. Alternatives: OrderBy at query time (pay per sort, keep O(1) storage), PriorityQueue for min/max-only needs (cheaper than full ordering), and database ORDER BY instead of in-memory sorts for large sets.
internalWorking: Red-black trees rebalance on insert (rotations, O(log n)); SortedList inserts via Array.Copy shifts then binary-searches reads (Array.BinarySearch); GetViewBetween returns a windowed view (no copy) tracking version for fail-fast.
realWorldUsage: Schedulers and calendars, leaderboards, config tables, time-series windows, and autocomplete prefix ranges.
commonMistake: SortedList for insert-heavy flows (quadratic memmoves — use SortedDictionary), SortedDictionary for pure lookups (Dictionary is O(1) — order you never use is pure tax), and mutating keys in ways that break comparer order (same lost-entry class as hash mutation).
technicalConversation: Ask whether their 'sorted' data is sorted at rest or at query — build-once/read-many favors SortedList, evolving sets favor trees, one-off views favor OrderBy.
interviewFollowUp: How does GetViewBetween avoid copying, and what invalidates the view?
keyTakeaway: Trees for evolving order, arrays for frozen order, sets for ordered uniqueness. Unused order is a tax — don't pay it.

questionText: How does ArrayPool<T> work, and when should you rent instead of allocate?
shortAnswer: ArrayPool<T>.Shared rents arrays from per-core buckets (power-of-two sizes) and Return gives them back — eliminating Gen0 churn for buffers. Rent for short-lived scratch buffers (I/O, parsing, crypto); never for long-lived storage, and always Return in finally (optionally cleared for secrets).
detailedAnswer: Rent(minLength) returns an array with Length >= requested (usually larger — use only the first N, track count separately!). Buckets per core × size class avoid contention; oversized requests (>1MB default max) allocate unpooled. Patterns: using var owner = MemoryPool<T>.Shared.Rent(n) (IMemoryOwner auto-returns on Dispose — preferred), or try/finally with ArrayPool Return. Return(array, clearArray: true) zeroes for secrets/PII (pooled memory otherwise leaks previous contents — a security review point). Rules: don't hold past method scope (pool starvation), don't Return twice (corrupts the pool — undetectable, catastrophic), don't assume Length == requested, don't store references beyond Return (use-after-return reads another tenant's leftover data). Kestrel/System.Text.Json rent internally — following the same pattern aligns with the platform. Measure: Gen0 collections drop in profiles; allocation profilers show buffer rentals replacing new byte[]. When pooling isn't enough, stackalloc spans (<1KB) or RecyclableMemoryStream (large streams) complete the toolkit.
internalWorking: Per-core bucket arrays (16 buckets, sizes 16..1M); Rent takes first free or allocates; Return pushes back (bucket cap ~8 per class, overflow dropped to GC). No clearing by default (perf) — clearArray:true costs a memset. TLS + partition locking keeps Rent/Return near-lock-free.
realWorldUsage: Socket loops, file hashing, image pipelines, compression, serializers, and any per-request scratch above ~1KB in hot paths.
commonMistake: Using buffer.Length instead of bytes-read (garbage tail), forgetting Return (slow pool starvation leak), double-Return (pool corruption), holding rented buffers in fields (lifetime violation), and pooling tiny arrays (overhead exceeds benefit — stackalloc instead).
technicalConversation: Ask what happens to pooled PII buffers without clearing — the next renter reads the previous tenant's data, which makes clearArray a security control, not an optimization.
interviewFollowUp: Why must you never use buffer.Length as the data length after Rent?
keyTakeaway: Rent short-lived buffers, use slices, Return in finally, clear secrets. Never store, double-return, or trust Length.

questionText: How do large collections interact with the Large Object Heap, and how do you avoid LOH pain?
shortAnswer: Objects ≥85KB land on the LOH: collected rarely (with Gen2) and historically fragmenting. Avoid by chunking large lists (e.g. pages of 10k), pooling buffers, streaming (IAsyncEnumerable) instead of materializing, and paging at the source (DB).
detailedAnswer: A List<byte> growing past 85k total, a 100k-element int[] (400KB), or a big string all allocate on the LOH. Consequences: collection only during Gen2 (expensive, infrequent), fragmentation from pinned/mixed lifetimes (holes that can't compact on older runtimes; .NET 8+ compacts LOH on demand but it costs a full blocking Gen2), and address-space pressure on 32-bit. Detection: GC counters (LOH size), dotnet-gcdump showing fragmented free space, Gen2 frequency spikes. Fixes in order: (1) don't materialize — stream (yield/IAsyncEnumerable) and page queries (Take/Skip or keyset); (2) chunk — List<List<T>> pages or Channel batches keep each allocation small and Gen0-collectible; (3) pool — ArrayPool/MemoryPool for buffers; (4) reuse — Clear() lists instead of re-allocating; (5) compact deliberately — GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode = CompactOnce sparingly (a latency hit you schedule). String-specific: StringBuilder with capacity, string.Create with exact length, and interpolated handlers over +=. Also watch pinned LOH (fixed/GCHandle on big arrays blocks compaction around them) and finalizable wrappers holding LOH (double whammy: delayed + big).
internalWorking: LOH segments allocate bump-pointer like Gen0 but sweep rarely; free-list holes from dead objects fragment the segment (older CLR never compacted; modern compacts only on request due to cost). 85,000-byte threshold is per-object (array payload + header). Pinning plugs (GCHandles) freeze regions during compaction.
realWorldUsage: File/report generation, export endpoints, ETL batches, image processing, and any ToList() over unbounded queries.
commonMistake: ToList() on unbounded queries (the classic production LOH bomb), 85KB+ string building without capacity, per-request 100k arrays (pool or chunk), and 'fixing' with GC.Collect (forces the expensive Gen2 you wanted to avoid).
technicalConversation: Ask what their largest endpoint returns and how — ToList-then-serialize of unbounded data is the LOH incident waiting to happen; streaming/paging is the review ask.
interviewFollowUp: Why is 81920 a meaningful buffer size, and what changes at 85000?
keyTakeaway: 85KB+ objects live long and fragment. Stream, chunk, pool — never materialize unbounded data.

questionText: How do EnsureCapacity, TrimExcess, and capacity planning prevent collection churn?
shortAnswer: EnsureCapacity grows once to the known size (no repeated doubling); TrimExcess shrinks spare buffer after bulk ops; planning capacity from expected counts removes growth copies entirely. Together they turn O(n) reallocations into one.
detailedAnswer: List<T>/Dictionary/HashSet/Stack/Queue all expose constructors or EnsureCapacity(count): when the final size is predictable (row counts, file lines, batch sizes), pre-size and every Add is a plain store — zero copies, zero Gen0 spikes. Dictionary needs capacity AND comparer up front (resize rehashes everything — the most expensive growth here). After bulk load-then-trim lifecycles (startup caches, import batches), TrimExcess() releases the doubling slack (List halves bookkeeping; Dictionary rehashes smaller). Collection expressions and ToList() already size exactly when the source exposes Count (TryGetNonEnumeratedCount fast path) — another reason to prefer Count-known sources. Measurement: allocation profilers showing sawtooth growth arrays, or Gen0 spikes correlated with loads. Anti-patterns: capacity 0 + millions of adds (log-factor copies), TrimExcess per request (rehash churn — trim at lifecycle points only), and over-sizing 'just in case' (permanent waste × instance count — caches with 10x slack are a memory leak in a trench coat). Rule: size from data (counts, limits, page sizes), trim at rest points, never guess-and-forget.
internalWorking: EnsureCapacity computes the next doubling ≥ target and performs a single Array.Copy (or rehash). ToList over ICollection<T> allocates exactly Count (no growth at all). TrimExcess sets capacity = count (with a small threshold to avoid thrash on tiny lists).
realWorldUsage: Import pipelines, cache warmup, report builders, test-data factories, and response assembly for known page sizes.
commonMistake: Default capacity + huge loads (the sawtooth), TrimExcess in request paths (per-request rehash), and magic-number capacities that rot as data grows (derive from counts/limits).
technicalConversation: Ask where their capacities come from — 'default' means unmeasured; counts, limits, and page sizes are the honest answers.
interviewFollowUp: Why is Dictionary growth more expensive than List growth, and what does that imply for warmup code?
keyTakeaway: Size from data, grow once, trim at rest. Capacity planning deletes entire classes of allocations.

questionText: How do you implement an LRU cache with Dictionary + LinkedListNode, and why that pairing?
shortAnswer: Dictionary maps keys to LinkedList nodes for O(1) lookup; the linked list orders by recency (move-to-front on hit, evict from tail). Get/put stay O(1) with O(1) eviction — the pairing gives hash speed plus positional control no single structure offers.
detailedAnswer: Structure: Dictionary<K, LinkedListNode<Entry>> index + LinkedList<Entry> order. Get(key): index hit → list.Remove(node) + AddFirst(node) (O(1) given the node — no search) → return value; miss → load, AddFirst, index[key] = node. Put: if exists update + move-front; else add-front, and while Count > capacity remove Last (O(1) tail eviction). Why not one structure: Dictionary can't order by recency; LinkedList can't search by key; List gives O(n) eviction. Threading: lock the pair (both mutate together — striped locks only if sharded by key hash). MemoryCache (Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Memory) exists — hand-roll only for bounded-LRU specifics (size accounting, custom eviction callbacks, no timers): SizeLimit + eviction callbacks cover most needs. Expiry: store timestamps, evict lazily on access + periodic sweep (avoid timer-per-entry). Metrics: hit rate (the only number that matters), evictions, load latency. Testing: deterministic sequences (fill → touch → overflow → assert evicted set) plus concurrency smoke (Parallel adds, count never exceeds cap).
internalWorking: LinkedListNode add/remove rewires 4 pointers (no copies, no search when the node is known). Dictionary probes hash as usual. Combined per-op cost: one hash + constant pointer work — true O(1) with small constants.
realWorldUsage: Response caches, parsed-template stores, connection pools with idle eviction, thumbnail caches, and DNS/route memoization.
commonMistake: Forgetting to update both structures together (ghost entries), evicting without capacity check races (lock the pair), and reimplementing when MemoryCache.SizeLimit + callbacks suffice.
technicalConversation: Ask when they would NOT hand-roll — MemoryCache with SizeLimit covers most bounded caches; custom LRU earns its keep only with special eviction or accounting rules.
interviewFollowUp: How would you add per-entry TTL without a timer per entry?
keyTakeaway: Dictionary for lookup, linked list for order, nodes as the bridge. O(1) everything, evict from the tail.
